title: Finding a Voice in the Writing Process Classroom and Beyond
author: Terry Underwood
summary: Underwood proposes audience as the organizing key to balanced writing instruction, arguing that writers who write for a null audience lose their voice and never learn to revise. He draws on his own teaching of community college composition and fourth-grade writing workshop, including a Parent Reader program that gave children real feedback on drafts. He traces how the American habit of teaching the paragraph and five-paragraph essay strips away audience and purpose. Through Piaget's reflective abstraction he distinguishes a fictional audience from a theoretical audience built out of experiences with real readers. He applies the lens to the firing of a high school principal over a newsletter and to a NAEP framework revision, calling both cases of a hegemonic audience that takes over the writer's voice. The post belongs in Learning & Curriculum because its core claim is a pedagogical one about teaching writing.
points: Audience works as a master organizer of the writing process, shaping invention, arrangement, style and delivery.
Writing without a real audience leaves students with no inner reader, so they cannot learn to read their own drafts and revise.
Textbook traditions that reduce writing to mastering the paragraph make audience and purpose irrelevant.
The Parent Reader program shows a concrete structure for authentic feedback, with receiving, pointing and wondering responses.
Experience with real readers lets students build a theoretical audience through reflective abstraction, a skill administrators writing under pressure also need.
quotes: Bringing a sense of audience opens up questions like what does this audience already know and believe? What arrangement of ideas would best serve my intention and their understanding? Too often, the only reader in the classroom writer’s mind is a teacher, and even that a shadowy presence.

Writers who never experience feedback from an audience for whom a text is shaped never have the chance to find out if decisions worked. Early and sustained experience with real audiences in the elementary years could produce enough reflective abstraction from empirical audiences to make unknown audiences not fictional but theoretical.

The difference between a theoretical audience and a fictional audience is night and day. A theoretical audience can be construed for a particular writing task through comparison and contrast of experiences with real audiences.

In my classroom, fourth graders wrote all day. The biggest challenge for me instructionally was to create conditions for real audiences to read their stuff, especially beyond the classroom. I actively worked to dissolve the examiner audience, the red pen, the metaphorical literacy hall monitor.

Structure, grammar and syntax, orthography, and punctuation are subject to deep and surface social, cultural, and linguistic rules and regulations that must be learned and followed in both academic and real world settings, but counting and highlighting errors doesn’t teach anyone anything about writing. I was reading Donald Graves as I looked for guidance, and he insisted that firsthand contact with an authentic reader where a writer finds out what happened when a reader took up the writing—that’s the moment of electric shock.

Training the parents and the writers in the same feedback protocol cemented the distinction between formative and summative feedback. Parents overlooked spelling, handwriting, and punctuation—those belonged to the teacher. They were readers, letting the writers take a look inside their heads while they were reading.
